==Early life and education==
Garfield was born in 1925 in New York City as Eugene Eli Garfinkle,<ref name=obit/> his mother being of [[Lithuanian Jews|Lithuanian Jewish]] ancestry.<ref>{{cite web|title=Deeds and Dreams of Eugene Garfield|url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/papers/chemicalintelligencerp26y1999.pdf|work=[[University of Pennsylvania]]|access-date=October 16, 2013|archive-date=November 17, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231117210312/http://www.garfield.library.upenn.edu/papers/chemicalintelligencerp26y1999.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=his-bio>{{cite book|title=World Encyclopedia of Library and Information Services|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HSFu99FCJwQC&pg=PA313|access-date=October 14, 2013|isbn = 9780838906095|year = 1993 | last1=Wedgeworth | first1=Robert }}</ref> His parents were second generation immigrants living in [[East Bronx]] in New York City.<ref name=":0" /> He studied at the [[University of Colorado]] and [[University of California, Berkeley]] before getting a Bachelor of Science degree in [[chemistry]] from [[Columbia University]] in 1949.<ref name=infoplease>{{cite 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170303050720/http://www.infoplease.com/biography/var/eugenegarfield.html|archive-date=March 3, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=timeshigher>{{cite 2017|url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/citation-analytics-pioneer-eugene-garfield-dies-aged-91|website=[[Times Higher Education]]|first=John|last=Elmes|year=2017|title=Citation analytics ==Career and research==
Working as a laboratory assistant at Columbia University after his graduation, Garfield indexed all previously synthesized compounds so that not to remake them, which helped him understand that his inclination to information towards science was bigger than towards chemistry. 

In 1951, he got a position at the Welch Medical Library at [[Johns Hopkins University]] in Baltimore, Maryland, where most of the [[United States National Library of Medicine|National Library of Medicine]] information systems were developed. There he built search and cataloging system methods using [[Punched card|punch-cards]]. In 1953, at the First Symposium on Machine Methods in Scientific Documentation, Garfield got introduced to [[Shepard's Citations]].<ref name=":0" />

In 1960, Garfield founded the [[Institute for Scientific Information|Institute for Scientific Information (ISI)]], which was located in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.<ref name="OralHistory" /> In the 1990s, ISI was faced with bankruptcy and was acquired by JPT Holdings who later sold it to Thomson (Thomas Business Information) where it formed a major part of the science division of [[Thomson Reuters]]. In October 2016 Thomson Reuters completed the sale of its intellectual property and science division; it is now known as [[Clarivate Analytics]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://clarivate.com/news/ip-and-science-launched-as-independent-company/|title=Acquisition of the Thomson Reuters Intellectual Property and Science Business by Onex and Baring Asia Completed|website=clarivate.com|access-date=March 2, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170703151258/http://clarivate.com/news/ip-and-science-launched-as-independent-company/|archive-date=July 3, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Garfield was responsible for many innovative bibliographic products, including ''[[Current Contents]]'', the ''[[Science Citation Index]]'' (SCI), and other citation databases, the ''[[Journal Citation Reports]]'', and ''Index Chemicus''. He was the founding editor and publisher of ''[[The Scientist (magazine)|The Scientist]]'', a news magazine for life scientists.<ref name=":0" /> In 2003, the [[University of South Florida]] School of Information was honored to have him as lecturer for the [[Alice G. Smith Lecture]]. In 2007, he launched [[Histcite]], a bibliometric analysis and visualization software package.

Following ideas inspired by [[Vannevar Bush]]'s highly cited 1945 article ''[[As We May Think]]'', Garfield undertook the development of a comprehensive [[citation index]] showing the propagation of scientific thinking; he started the [[Institute for Scientific Information]] in 1956 (it was sold to the [[Thomson Corporation]] in 1992<ref>{{cite journal | title = Thomson Corporation acquired ISI | journal = [[Online (magazine)|Online]] | url =http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-12394745.html | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20130515103411/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-12394745.html | url-status =usurped | archive-date =May 15, 2013 |date = July 1992 | via = [[HighBeam Research]] | url-access = subscription | access-date = January 15, 2015}}</ref>). According to Garfield, "the citation index ... may help a historian to measure the influence of an article — that is, its 'impact factor'".<ref>{{cite journal |author=Garfield E |s2cid=5902162 |title=Citation indexes for science: A new dimension in documentation through association of ideas |journal=Science |volume=122 |issue=3159 |pages=108–11 |year=1955 |doi=10.1126/science.122.3159.108 |pmid=14385826|bibcode=1955Sci...122..108G }}</ref> The creation of the ''Science Citation Index'' made it possible to calculate [[impact factor]],<ref name="pmid16391221">{{cite journal |author=Garfield E |s2cid=31183037 |title=The history and meaning of the journal impact factor |journal=JAMA |volume=295 |issue=1 |pages=90–3 |year=2006 |pmid=16391221 |doi=10.1001/jama.295.1.90|bibcode=2006JAMA..295...90G }}</ref> which ostensibly measures the importance of scientific journals. It led to the unexpected discovery that a few journals like ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' and ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' were core for all of [[hard science]]. The same pattern does not happen with the humanities or the social sciences.<ref name="Buranyi">{{cite news|last1=Buranyi|first1=Stephen|title=Is the staggeringly profitable business of scientific publishing bad for science?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/jun/27/profitable-business-scientific-publishing-bad-for-science|access-date=September 15, 2017|work=The Guardian|date=June 27, 2017}}</ref><ref name="Goodall">{{cite news|last1=Goodall|first1=Amanda|last2=Oswald|first2=Andrew|title=Do the social sciences need a shake-up?|work=THE World University Rankings|url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/features/do-the-social-sciences-need-a-shake-up/2016165.article|date=October 9, 2014|access-date=September 15, 2017}}</ref>

His entrepreneurial flair in having turned what was, at least at the time, an obscure and specialist metric into a highly profitable business has been noted.<ref name=annurev/> A scientometric analysis of his top fifty cited papers has been conducted.<ref>Pandey, Shriram, and Dinesh K. Gupta. 2021. “A Scientometric Analysis and Visualization of the 50 Highly Cited Papers of Eugene Garfield.” ''Annals of Library & Information Studies'' 68 (2): 135–44.</ref>

Garfield's work led to the development of several [[information retrieval]] algorithms, like the [[HITS algorithm]] and [[PageRank]]. Both use the structured citation between websites through hyperlinks. Google co-founders [[Larry Page]] and [[Sergey Brin]] acknowledged Garfield in their development of PageRank, the algorithm that powers their company's search engine.<ref name=annurev>{{cite web|url=https://annualreviewsnews.org/2017/02/27/eugene-garfield-1925-2017/|title=Eugene Garfield – 1925–2017 – a life of impact|website=annualreviewsnews.org|first=Richard|last=Gallagher|year=2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170228172321/https://annualreviewsnews.org/2017/02/27/eugene-garfield-1925-2017/|archive-date=February 28, 2017}}</ref> Garfield published over 1,000 essays.

==Honors and awards==
Garfield was honored with the [[Award of Merit - Association for Information Science and Technology|Award of Merit]] from the [[Association for Information Science and Technology]] in 1975.

He was awarded the [[John Price Wetherill Medal]] in 1984,<ref name="OralHistory">{{cite book |last1=Williams |first1=Robert V. |title=Eugene Garfield, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Robert V. Williams at Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on 29 July 1997 |url=https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/papers/oralhistorybywilliams.pdf |place=Philadelphia, PA |publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] |date=July 29, 1997 |archive-date=December 6, 2006 |access-date=November 16, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061206115841/http://garfield.library.upenn.edu/papers/oralhistorybywilliams.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> the [[Derek de Solla Price Memorial Medal]] in 1984,<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://issi-society.org/awards/derek-de-solla-price-memorial-medal/ |title = Derek de Solla Price Memorial Medal}}</ref> and the Miles Conrad Award in 1985.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.niso.org/awards/MCA | title=Miles Conrad Award and Lectures &#124; NISO website }}</ref> He was also awarded the [[Richard J. Bolte Sr. Award]] in 2007.<ref name="Bolte">{{cite web|title=Richard J. Bolte Sr. Award for Supporting Industries|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/richard-j-bolte-sr-award-for-supporting-industries|website=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=February 6, 2018|date=May 31, 2016}}</ref> He was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] that same year.<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Eugene+Garfield&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=May 14, 2021|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> 

The [[Association for Library and Information Science Education]] has a fund for doctoral research through an award named after Garfield.

==Criticism==
Writing in ''Physiology News'', No. 69, Winter 2007, [[David Colquhoun]] of the Department of Pharmacology, [[University College London]], described the "[[impact factor]]," a method for comparing scholarly journals, as "the invention of Eugene Garfield, a man who has done enormous harm to true science." Colquhoun ridiculed C. Hoeffel's assertion that Garfield's impact factor "has the advantage of already being in existence and is, therefore, a good technique for scientific evaluation" by saying, "you can't get much dumber than that. It is a 'good technique' because it is already in existence? There is something better. Read the papers."

==Personal life==
Garfield is survived by a wife, three sons, a daughter, two granddaughters, and two great-grandchildren.<ref name=obit/><ref name="OralHistory"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.webofstories.com/people/eugene.garfield|title= Eugene Garfield tells his life story (video)|website=webofstories.com}}</ref>
